items.prompt: What is a "time series"?
choices: A sequence of values recorded at regular time intervals, where the order matters
Any list of numbers, regardless of when they were recorded
A single measurement taken once, with no history attached
A chart showing the relationship between two unrelated variables
items.explanation: A time series is specifically ordered by regular time intervals (weekly, daily, hourly) — an unordered list of numbers or a single one-off measurement isn't a time series.

items.prompt: In the Scenario, what makes the twelve weeks of signup counts a time series rather than just a list of numbers?
choices: Each count is tied to a specific, regularly spaced week, and the order of those weeks matters
There happen to be exactly twelve of them
The numbers are all whole numbers rather than decimals
They were all measured on the same day
items.explanation: What makes it a time series is the regular weekly spacing and the fact that order carries meaning — shuffling the twelve numbers would destroy the trend information entirely.

items.prompt: What's the difference between "trend" and "noise" in a time series?
choices: Trend is the underlying direction the data is actually moving; noise is random fluctuation that doesn't reflect a real change in direction
Trend only applies to weekly data; noise only applies to daily data
Trend is measured in absolute numbers; noise is measured in percentages
There's no real difference — they're two names for the same thing
items.explanation: Trend and noise are distinct concepts — trend is the real underlying direction, noise is fluctuation around that direction that doesn't represent a genuine shift.

items.prompt: In the Scenario, the PM read weeks 11-12's jump as pure trend. What did that reading ignore?
choices: The possibility that some or all of the jump was noise — like a single viral post — rather than a genuine change in the underlying growth rate
The fact that signups can never actually increase week over week
The exact date the two weeks occurred on
Nothing — a two-week jump is always pure trend by definition
items.explanation: L1 is explicit that reading a two-point jump as pure trend ignores the real possibility that some or all of it is noise, such as a one-off viral event.

items.prompt: What is "extrapolation"?
choices: Projecting a fitted trend forward past the range of data actually observed
Calculating the average of a set of already-observed values
Filling in a missing value between two data points that were already measured
Rounding a number to a fixed number of decimal places
items.explanation: Extrapolation specifically means projecting beyond the observed range — not averaging, not filling in missing interior values, and not rounding.

items.prompt: Per L1, does extrapolation get riskier or safer the further out you project?
choices: Riskier — especially when the trend was fit from very few points, or from points near the edge of the data that happen to be unusual
Safer — the further out you project, the more the noise averages itself out automatically
It stays exactly equally risky no matter how far out you project
Risk only depends on how many decimal places the forecast is reported with
items.explanation: L1 explicitly states extrapolation gets riskier the further out you project, especially from a trend fit on few or unusual points.

items.prompt: What does "linear regression (least squares)" do?
choices: Fits a straight line through a full set of data points by minimizing the sum of squared differences between the line and each actual point
Picks the two most recent data points and draws a line through only those
Sorts the data points from smallest to largest
Removes every data point that doesn't fit a straight line
items.explanation: Least squares specifically minimizes the total squared distance across every point in the dataset — not just the two most recent, and not by deleting anything.

items.prompt: How does least-squares regression differ from the naive two-point method the PM used in the Scenario?
choices: It fits a line using every point in the dataset at once, rather than just the two most recent ones
It only ever produces a flat, zero-slope line
It requires manually removing the two most recent points before fitting
It's mathematically identical to the two-point method, just with a different name
items.explanation: The defining difference is using the full dataset to fit the line, rather than reading a rate of change off just the two most recent points.

items.prompt: Per the Scenario, how many of the twelve available weeks did the PM's forecast actually use?
choices: Two — weeks 11 and 12
All twelve weeks
Ten — every week except weeks 11 and 12
The Scenario doesn't specify how many weeks were used
items.explanation: The Scenario is explicit that the forecast used exactly two numbers — week 11 and week 12 — out of the twelve weeks of data actually available.

items.prompt: What event does the Scenario mention right before the two-week jump the PM extrapolated from?
choices: A post about the product went viral
The company hired a new marketing team
A competitor shut down
The Scenario doesn't mention any specific event
items.explanation: The Scenario states a post about the product went viral right before the jump — a plausible one-off cause the naive forecast treated as ongoing growth instead.

items.prompt: Per L2, why can't two points alone tell you whether data follows a real trend?
choices: Any two points define a perfectly straight line by definition, regardless of whether the broader data actually behaves that way
Two points is technically too many — only a single point can define a trend
Two points always overestimate the trend, never underestimate it
There's no issue at all — two points are just as reliable as twelve
items.explanation: L2 makes the point that any two points trivially define a line — that mathematical fact says nothing about whether the underlying data genuinely moves that way.

items.prompt: Per L2, what does least-squares regression do differently from reading a rate off the two most recent points?
choices: It fits one line by minimizing the total squared distance to every point in the dataset at once, not just the last two
It always produces the exact same slope as the two-point method, just phrased differently
It ignores the two most recent points entirely and only uses the oldest data
It requires collecting new data before it can run at all
items.explanation: L2 defines least-squares regression as fitting through every point at once via minimizing squared distance — a genuinely different computation from a two-point rate.

items.prompt: Per L2, does fitting a regression on all twelve weeks fully solve the naive forecast's problem?
choices: Only partially — weeks 11 and 12 sit at the edge of a small dataset and still pull the fitted line toward themselves more than an ordinary week would
Yes, completely — once regression is used, every point has exactly equal influence over the result
No, regression makes the problem strictly worse than the naive method
Regression can't be run on this data at all because of the spike
items.explanation: L2 is explicit that regression only partially fixes the issue — points at the edge of a small dataset still carry outsized influence, or "leverage," on the fitted line.

items.prompt: Per L2, why does squaring distances (rather than just averaging them) matter for how outliers affect a fit?
choices: Squaring means points far from the line count more heavily than points close to it, so an outlying point pulls the fit toward itself disproportionately
Squaring makes every point count exactly equally, canceling out any outlier's influence
Squaring is only a cosmetic choice with no effect on which line gets fit
Squaring is used purely to keep all distances positive, with no effect on relative weighting
items.explanation: L2 explains that squaring distances weights points far from the line more heavily — which is exactly why an outlier near the edge of the data has outsized pull on the fit.

items.prompt: Per L2, does a real spike in the data mean it should simply be deleted before fitting a trend?
choices: Not necessarily — a real spike might signal something worth investigating; the point is that it shouldn't be blindly folded into the trend line either
Yes — any point that doesn't fit the existing pattern should always be deleted
Yes, but only if the spike happens in the very first week of the data
No — every single point must always be included in the fit with no exceptions, no matter the context
items.explanation: L2 explicitly rejects "just delete the outlier" as the takeaway — a spike may be worth investigating on its own terms, separate from whether it should dominate the trend estimate.

items.prompt: Per L2, is projecting a fitted line to week 13 as risky as projecting it to week 52?
choices: No — week 13 stays close to the observed range (weeks 1-12), while week 52 assumes the same trend holds for forty more weeks nothing in the data has confirmed
Yes — every future week carries exactly the same risk once a line is fit
Week 52 is actually safer, since regression becomes more accurate the further it's projected
Risk only depends on the slope of the line, never on how far out the forecast goes
items.explanation: L2 is explicit that a forecast just past the observed range and one forty weeks out do not carry the same risk, even from the identical fitted line.

items.prompt: Per L2, what kinds of real-world changes are invisible to a straight line fit purely on past data?
choices: New competitors, seasonality, market saturation, or the trend itself changing
Nothing is invisible to a fitted line — it accounts for every possible future factor automatically
Only changes to the exact numeric values already in the dataset
Regression can only miss changes that happen on a leap year
items.explanation: L2 lists exactly these examples — competitors, seasonality, saturation, or a genuine trend shift — as real changes a line fit on past data alone cannot see coming.

items.prompt: Per L2's failure modes, what's wrong with computing a "trend" from only the two most recent points?
choices: Any two points define a perfectly straight line by definition — that says nothing about whether the broader data actually behaves that way
Nothing is wrong with it — two points are described as the ideal amount of data for a trend
The issue only applies when the two points are exactly one week apart
It's wrong only because computers can't perform division on two numbers
items.explanation: L2's failure modes table makes this exact point — two points trivially define a line, which says nothing about whether that reflects real underlying behavior.

items.prompt: Per L2's failure modes, what's the risk of reporting a regression's forecast without checking its fit quality?
choices: A weak fit means the line leaves most of the variation unexplained, and the forecast built on it inherits that uncertainty
There's no risk — every regression fit is equally trustworthy regardless of how well it matches the data
The only risk is that the forecast might come out as a negative number
Fit quality only matters for datasets with more than a hundred points
items.explanation: L2's failure modes table warns that a forecast inherits whatever uncertainty comes from a weak fit — reporting the number alone hides that uncertainty.

items.prompt: Implement linearRegression(xs, ys), returning { slope, intercept } for the least-squares line through the given points.

tests.description: a perfect line (y = 2x) fits with slope 2 and intercept 0
the same perfect line has an intercept of 0
a noisy dataset fits the least-squares slope and intercept

items.explanation: The slope is the covariance between x and y (how much they move together) divided by the variance of x (how spread out x is) — the intercept is whatever value makes the line pass through the average point exactly.
items.reference:
📏 num — how much each point's x and y deviate from the mean, together
📐 den — how spread out the x values are

Why: dividing correlated spread by x's own spread gives the line's slope; the intercept then anchors it through the average point.

items.prompt: Implement linearRegression(xs, ys), returning { slope, intercept } for the least-squares line through the given points.

tests.description: a perfect line (y = 2x + 1) fits with slope 2
the same perfect line has intercept 1
a different noisy dataset fits the least-squares slope

items.explanation: Same formula regardless of the specific dataset: covariance between x and y divided by the variance of x gives the slope, and the intercept anchors the line through the average point.
items.reference:
📏 num — how much each point's x and y deviate from the mean, together
📐 den — how spread out the x values are

Why: dividing correlated spread by x's own spread gives the line's slope; the intercept then anchors it through the average point.

items.prompt: Implement rSquared(xs, ys, slope, intercept), measuring how well the given line fits the data (1 = perfect fit, 0 = no better than the average).

tests.description: a line that passes through every point exactly has R² of 1
a partially-fitting line has R² between 0 and 1

items.explanation: ssRes measures how far the line's predictions are from the actual points; ssTot measures how far the actual points are from their own average. A line that predicts every point exactly has ssRes of 0, making R² equal 1.
items.reference:
❌ ssRes — squared error the line's predictions still leave behind
📉 ssTot — squared spread of the actual data around its own average

Why: R² compares how much error the line leaves versus how much spread existed to begin with — near 1 means the line explains almost all of it.

tests.description: a line that passes through every point exactly has R² of 1, on a different dataset
a different partially-fitting line has a high but non-perfect R²

items.explanation: Same formula regardless of dataset: comparing leftover squared error (ssRes) against total squared spread (ssTot) tells you what fraction of the data's variation the line actually explains.
